insights.text: Mercedes had the fastest average team pace of the season opener, Ferrari 0.46s back in 2nd — and Mercedes would go on to lead team pace in 11 of the season's first 17 sessions. Red Bull, despite Verstappen's individual pace, was only 4th as a team, a pattern that held all year: Red Bull never once topped the team-pace table, because Hadjar's number drags their average down.

George Russell won the race despite only the 2nd-quickest individual pace, 0.013s behind team-mate Antonelli — the first of four 2026 wins for Russell where he didn't have the fastest lap in the field.
Haas had its best team-pace showing of the season here and in the following race in China (both 5th) — every other 2026 race, it settled into the 8th-9th range instead.

Fernando Alonso beat Lance Stroll by 0.67s, more than double Aston Martin's usual 2026 gap and their widest margin of the season so far. Max Verstappen's 1.10s margin over Isack Hadjar was similarly one of Red Bull's biggest of the year — bigger than every other race except the Zandvoort sprint, where a stand-in team-mate was in the other car.
Esteban Ocon had the 7th-quickest pace but finished 11th, while Alexander Albon and Sergio Perez both finished four places better than their raw pace suggested.
The season opener's pace order was unusually sensitive to how traffic gets modeled — a 3-place reshuffle between variants, on the high end for 2026.

George Russell won the sprint despite only the 4th-quickest pace (0.28s off McLaren) — the second of his four 2026 wins that didn't come from the fastest car.

An unusually chaotic sprint for team-mates — five different teams (Alpine, Aston Martin, Cadillac, Racing Bulls and Williams) all posted their widest gap of the season in this one race.
The one exception to Red Bull's usual pattern: Isack Hadjar actually out-paced Max Verstappen here, by 0.21s — the only session all season that's happened — before retiring at lap 20 of 23.
Isack Hadjar's retirement aside, Esteban Ocon and Valtteri Bottas both finished several places ahead of what their raw pace predicted.

Antonelli won with the outright fastest pace, in stark contrast to McLaren's own drivers, who had led the field on raw pace just one day earlier.
Montreal showed essentially no tyre degradation this year — the flattest curve of any 2026 race, with tyres barely slowing (and by the model's math even marginally speeding up) with age.
Track temperature mattered more at Montreal than anywhere else this season — hotter track correlated with meaningfully faster laps, the strongest such relationship of any 2026 race.

Both George Russell (retiring lap 30 of 68 after the 2nd-best pace) and Lando Norris (retiring lap 39 after 7th-best pace) had strong races ended early, while Liam Lawson and Lance Stroll both finished well clear of what their raw pace predicted.

insights.text: Monaco's pace numbers this year are essentially unreliable — the model explains almost none of the lap-time variation, the lowest of any 2026 race, and the fitted order can swing by as much as 17 grid places depending on modeling choices. Read every number here as a rough approximation.

Ferrari edged out Mercedes for fastest team pace by a mere 0.026s — but Antonelli won anyway. Ferrari had the fastest average team pace twice this season (here and at Zandvoort) and converted neither into a win, the opposite problem from its two actual wins, both of which came in races Mercedes' team pace was faster.

Running wheel-to-wheel cost far more time at Monaco than anywhere else this season — the model's cost of a close battle was more than five times the season median, unsurprising for the tightest track on the calendar.

Lando Norris (2nd-best pace) retired just past half distance (lap 44 of 78), and Charles Leclerc (3rd-best) retired late enough (lap 65 of 78) to fall short of classification; Sergio Perez, by contrast, finished 10th despite only the 20th-quickest pace.

Monaco also produced the season's widest team-mate gap yet at both Mercedes and McLaren — but given how unreliable this race's overall fit is, that's as likely to be noise from too few clean laps as a genuine gap.

insights.text: Mercedes' team-pace lead was its usual comfortable self here (0.04s over Ferrari, McLaren 3rd within 0.25s) — Red Bull was 4th, its rank essentially unchanged from its season-typical spot despite Liam Lawson standing in for the injured Hadjar.

George Russell won despite only the 4th-quickest underlying pace — his fourth win of the season, and the fourth time in a row it's come without the fastest car, a case of track position and racecraft beating raw speed.

Zandvoort's sprint showed the strongest reverse fuel effect of any 2026 session — lap times got faster, not slower, as the short race went on, the clearest version of a pattern seen in every 2026 sprint, where 20-odd laps just isn't enough fuel burn for the usual penalty to show up.

Ferrari (Leclerc over Hamilton) and Red Bull (Verstappen over stand-in Liam Lawson) both had wider-than-usual team-mate gaps this sprint — Red Bull's, at 1.15s, was in fact its widest of the whole season, though against a substitute rather than regular team-mate Hadjar.
Pierre Gasly finished 8th despite only the 11th-best pace, while Fernando Alonso and stand-in Liam Lawson both finished a few places worse than their pace alone predicted.

insights.text: Ferrari, McLaren and Mercedes were separated by just 0.094s for the top three team-pace spots at Zandvoort — the tightest three-way team-pace spread of any 2026 session — with Ferrari technically fastest. Red Bull, on Verstappen's home turf, was a distant 4th, 0.89s off.

Lando Norris won at Zandvoort despite McLaren having only the 2nd-fastest average team pace (0.08s behind Ferrari) — his own pace was the fastest in the field. Ferrari, meanwhile, led the team-pace table but didn't win, the second time that's happened this season (with Monaco).

Zandvoort punished cars stuck behind a backmarker more than any other 2026 race, but the moment a driver actually closed to within a second of that lapped car, the model found a net time gain — the biggest such swing in either direction all year. The approach costs a lot; the pass itself pays it back.

Aston Martin and Alpine both posted their widest team-mate gap of the season, while Williams' Albon-Sainz gap (0.02s) and Mercedes' Antonelli-Russell gap (0.03s) were both among the closest pairings anywhere in 2026. McLaren's gap (Norris 0.49s clear of Piastri) was on the wider side for them.

Charles Leclerc had the 2nd-quickest pace but finished 5th. Esteban Ocon retired at lap 53 of 72 — short of classification — despite 14th-best pace, and Sergio Perez finished four places better than his raw pace suggested.

insights.text: Red Bull's 4th-place team pace was shadowed incredibly closely by Alpine in 5th at Monza — just 0.024s back, a midfield team within a rounding error of a top-4 team on raw pace.
Antonelli won again — his 8th win of the season, and Mercedes' 12th win in 17 races — comfortably the dominant team-pace and results story of 2026 so far.

Liam Lawson had the 9th-quickest pace at Monza but finished 14th, and Yuki Tsunoda finished three places better than his pace rank (13th) suggested. Fernando Alonso's last-place finish reflects an early retirement (lap 24 of 53), not a pace collapse — he'd shown 18th-best pace beforehand.

Aston Martin's gap (Alonso 0.72s clear of Stroll, before his retirement) was its widest of the season, while Williams and Cadillac's team-mates were within a tenth of each other — both teams' tightest gap all year. McLaren's and Mercedes' gaps were unusually tight too (Norris 0.15s clear of Piastri, Antonelli 0.05s clear of Russell).

Lewis Hamilton's hard-tyre pace figure at Monza is extrapolated — Ferrari barely used that compound, so it's a model projection rather than a direct measurement, a pattern normally confined to the backmarkers.
The pace order at Monza was comparatively sensitive to model choices — a three-place reshuffle and a 0.7s swing in gaps depending on how traffic is treated, on the higher end for 2026.
